title: Prime numbers (math toolkit II)
syllabusUnit: Unit III: Number Theory & Primality Testing
covers: Primes, primality testing (Fermat/Miller-Rabin), factorization, Euler's totient, Fermat & Euler theorems
learningGoals: You will be able to explain why prime factorization is computationally hard.
You will be able to calculate Euler's totient function phi(n) for prime products.
You will be able to describe how Miller-Rabin tests large numbers for primality.

lessonCards.title: The Building Blocks of Math
lessonCards.analogy: Prime numbers are like indivisible chemical atoms: you can multiply atoms to make molecules, but splitting them is hard.
lessonCards.coreConcept: A prime number is divisible only by 1 and itself. Multiplying two large primes p and q takes milliseconds; finding p and q from their product n takes centuries.
lessonCards.example: Multiplying 61 * 53 = 3233 is easy; factoring 3233 by hand is slow.

lessonCards.title: Euler's Totient Function: phi(n)
lessonCards.analogy: Counting how many numbers on a clock face don't share any gears with the total hours.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Euler's totient phi(n) counts integers from 1 to n coprime to n. If p is prime, phi(p) = p - 1. For n = p * q, phi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1).

lessonCards.title: Fermat & Miller-Rabin Primality
lessonCards.analogy: Shaking a locked box: if it rattles a certain way, it's definitely not a solid stone.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Fermat's Little Theorem: a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p). Miller-Rabin tests odd numbers with random bases; passing 40 rounds makes probability of being composite < 2^-80.
lessonCards.example: Used by cryptographic libraries to generate safe 2048-bit prime numbers quickly.

questions.prompt: If p = 7 and q = 11 are two prime numbers, what is Euler's totient phi(n) where n = p * q = 77?
questions.explanation: For the product of two distinct primes: phi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1) = (7 - 1)(11 - 1) = 6 * 10 = 60.
wrongExplanations: 76 is (n - 1), which only applies if n itself were prime.
18 is p + q.
questions.realWorldExample: In RSA, phi(n) is secret and used to calculate the private decryption key d.

questions.prompt: What is the primary computational asymmetry that protects RSA encryption?
options: Multiplying primes is fast O(n^2), but factoring their product has no known polynomial-time classical algorithm
Prime numbers cannot be stored in RAM
questions.explanation: Multiplying large numbers is trivial, but the General Number Field Sieve (GNFS) takes sub-exponential time to factor large composite semiprimes.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The one-way trapdoor function relies on factoring difficulty.
Addition and subtraction execute in identical CPU cycles.
RAM stores any binary integer.
CPUs process odd and even numbers identically.
questions.realWorldExample: RSA-2048 keys require testing numbers with over 600 decimal digits.

questions.prompt: What does Fermat's Little Theorem state for any prime p and integer a not divisible by p?
questions.explanation: Fermat's Little Theorem states that if p is prime, then a^(p-1) mod p = 1 for any a where gcd(a, p) = 1.
wrongExplanations: Correct! a^(p - 1) mod p = 1 is Fermat's Little Theorem.
a^p mod p equals a, not 0.
Addition does not equal 1.
a * p mod p equals 0, not a.
questions.realWorldExample: Fermat's theorem forms the basis of Fermat and Miller-Rabin primality tests.

questions.prompt: Why does cryptography use probabilistic primality tests like Miller-Rabin instead of trial division?
options: Trial division would take billions of years on 1024-bit primes; Miller-Rabin finishes in milliseconds
Miller-Rabin only works on even numbers
Trial division requires supercomputers to add
questions.explanation: Trial division requires testing factors up to sqrt(n) (~2^512 operations). Miller-Rabin verifies primality probabilistically in polynomial time O(k * log^3 n).
wrongExplanations: Correct! Miller-Rabin generates cryptographically verified primes almost instantly.
Mathematical trial division is completely legal.
Miller-Rabin specifically tests odd candidates.
Trial division is slow due to operation count, not addition complexity.
questions.realWorldExample: OpenSSL uses Miller-Rabin iterations to generate RSA and Diffie-Hellman parameters.

options: A composite number that passes Fermat's primality test for all coprime bases
A number that cannot be factored
questions.explanation: Carmichael numbers (like 561) are composite numbers n that satisfy a^(n-1) = 1 (mod n) for all coprime a, fooling simple Fermat tests.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Carmichael numbers are pseudoprimes that fool Fermat's test, which is why Miller-Rabin is preferred.
Prime endings do not define pseudoprimes.
Carmichael numbers have known prime factors (561 = 3 * 11 * 17).
Primes in cryptography are positive integers.
questions.realWorldExample: The Miller-Rabin test checks square roots of 1 modulo n to catch all Carmichael numbers.

questions.prompt: If p is a prime number, what is the value of Euler's totient phi(p)?
questions.explanation: Since every number from 1 to p-1 is coprime to p, phi(p) = p - 1.
wrongExplanations: Correct! For any prime p, exactly p - 1 numbers are coprime to it.
p is not coprime to itself (gcd(p, p) = p).
p + 1 exceeds the count of integers up to p.
p / 2 is incorrect.

ashRecap: Primes are easy to multiply together, but nearly impossible to factor apart. That one-way trapdoor protects all public-key ciphers!
